California Dynamic Pricing Policy Context California is undertaking multiple policy actions to encourage load flexibility. This document provides information on policies through mid-2024. Table A1 describes many of these actions, listed by the main California institution involved and then chronologically. These institutions include the California legislature, the California Energy Commission (CEC), the CPUC, and the State’s Energy Code. Table A1: Recent California policies related to load flexibility California Institution Policy Details California Legislature SB100 (De León, Chapter 312, Statutes of 2018). Accelerates the existing Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) obligations for “retail sellers” in California. Adjustments are: (a) from 40% to 44% by 2024; (b) from 45% to 52% by 2027; and (c) from 50% to 60% by 2030. Requires that 100% of all California retail sales of electricity be supplied by RPS-eligible and zero-carbon resources by December 31, 2045. SB49 (Skinner, Chapter 697, Statutes of 2019). Modifies the CEC’s regulatory authority on establishing and periodically updating appliance energy efficiency standards to allow it to promote the diffusion and use of flexible demand technologies through “flexible demand appliance standards” (FDAS). AB205 (Chapter 61, Statutes of 2022). Repeals $10 cap on fixed charges in residential rates for IOU customers. Authorizes the CPUC to use fixed charges for any residential rate schedule, provided that charges are established on an income-graduated basis with no fewer than three income thresholds, and that low-income ratepayers realize a lower average monthly bill without making any chances in usage. Establishes the Distributed Electricity Backup Assets program to incentivize efficiency upgrades to power generators and new zero- or low-emission technologies at new and existing facilities as long as resulting assets are available to respond during an extreme event to support grid reliability.
